# Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations

Also called: SDF-based Neural Fields, Truncated SDF, Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF)

## Overview
Signed Distance Function (SDF) representations replace the standard NeRF density field $\sigma(\mathbf{x})$ with a continuous scalar field $s(\mathbf{x})$ representing the distance to the nearest surface, defining geometry via the zero-level set $\{\mathbf{x} \mid s(\mathbf{x}) = 0\}$ [S1]. This substitution addresses the geometric inaccuracy and surface holes typical of density-based NeRFs by providing a more explicit and smooth formulation of surfaces [S1]. Unlike standard NeRFs that model soft volumetric boundaries, SDF methods leverage the gradient of the distance function for surface normals and often employ truncation or ray-specific constraints to handle multi-object ambiguities [S1].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism involves predicting a continuous scalar field $s: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ (or its ray-conditioned variant) instead of a density $\sigma(\mathbf{x})$ [S1]. For any 3D point $\mathbf{x}$, the function value $s(\mathbf{x})$ represents the distance to the closest surface, with the sign conventionally negative inside the object and positive outside [S1].

To enable volumetric rendering, the predicted SDF value $s(\mathbf{x})$ is converted into a density $\sigma(\mathbf{x})$ [S1]. The specific conversion function is not detailed in the provided sources for all variants [G]. Standard differentiable rendering pipelines then integrate this density along rays to produce images, while the SDF structure encourages sharper, more coherent surface reconstructions compared to soft volumetric boundaries [S1].

The surface normal $\mathbf{n}$ is derived from the SDF gradient:
$$
\mathbf{n} = \frac{\nabla s(\mathbf{x})}{\|\nabla s(\mathbf{x})\|}
$$
This normal is used for shading, such as in Physically Based Rendering (PBR) models or incidence angle embeddings [S1].

## Subtopics

### [ProbeSDF](11363-probesdf.md)
ProbeSDF is a neural surface reconstruction method that decouples spatial and angular light field components using two volumetric grids of different resolutions to achieve real-time rendering and accelerated training. It addresses the computational bottleneck of standard SDF-based neural fields by replacing the core appearance MLP with a lightweight model that uses spherical harmonic light field probes for angular variation and planar factorized features for spatial texture. Unlike Plenoxels or 3D Gaussian Splatting which require significantly more parameters per voxel (27 and 48 respectively), ProbeSDF uses as few as four parameters per voxel while maintaining high expressiveness. See [ProbeSDF](11363-probesdf.md).

### [SDF-based Neural Fields](12947-sdf-based-neural-fields.md)
SDF-based Neural Fields replace the implicit density field of standard NeRFs with a Signed Distance Function (SDF) to provide a more explicit and smooth formulation of surfaces. This approach addresses the geometric inaccuracy and surface holes typical of density-based NeRFs by leveraging the zero-level set of the SDF to define geometry. See [SDF-based Neural Fields](12947-sdf-based-neural-fields.md).

### [Generalizable Implicit Reconstruction with SRDF](14760-generalizable-implicit-reconstruction-with-srdf.md)
VolRecon is a generalizable implicit reconstruction method that predicts a Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF) to reconstruct scenes with fine details and minimal noise from multi-view images. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like [SDF-based Neural Fields](12947-sdf-based-neural-fields.md) by combining local projection features aggregated via a view transformer with global shape priors from a coarse feature volume, processed by a ray transformer to resolve surface ambiguity. Unlike standard SDF approaches that define distance in any direction, SRDF constrains the distance measurement to the specific ray direction, enabling more robust surface localization along the viewing ray. See [Generalizable Implicit Reconstruction with SRDF](14760-generalizable-implicit-reconstruction-with-srdf.md).

### [SDF-based Neural Volume Rendering with PBR](15009-sdf-based-neural-volume-rendering-with-pbr.md)
This method integrates Signed Distance Function (SDF) representations for geometry with Physically Based Rendering (PBR) material models to achieve smoother geometric structures and accurate specular reflections, overcoming the coarse detail and foggy artifacts typical of standard NeRF. Unlike sibling methods such as [ProbeSDF](11363-probesdf.md) or [SDF-based Neural Fields](12947-sdf-based-neural-fields.md) which may focus primarily on geometry or general neural fields, this approach specifically decouples geometry (via SDF) from material appearance (via PBR), providing interpretable parameters for reflection and diffuse components. It builds on [Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations](12495-signed-distance-function-sdf-representations.md) by converting the SDF into a density field for volumetric integration while using the SDF gradient for surface normals required by the PBR model. See [SDF-based Neural Volume Rendering with PBR](15009-sdf-based-neural-volume-rendering-with-pbr.md).

### [RS-Recon](15321-rs-recon.md)
RS-Recon is a neural scene reconstruction method that replaces the standard Signed Distance Function (SDF) with a Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF) to model volume density, specifically addressing noise and inaccuracies in multi-object indoor scenes. Unlike SDF-based methods which consider surface points across the entire scene and may exhibit fluctuations leading to local minimum values, SRDF measures the shortest distance to the surface along a specific camera ray, eliminating the influence of surrounding surfaces not located on that ray. See [RS-Recon](15321-rs-recon.md).

#### Truncated SDF NeRF
- **Definition**: A method that replaces the density MLP with a truncated SDF MLP and computes pixel color as a weighted sum of sampled colors [S1].
- **Step**: Reconstruct the triangular mesh of the scene by using Marching Cubes [208] on the truncated SDF MLP [S1].
- **Formula**: Pixel color is computed as:
  $$
  C(r) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i c_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i}
  $$
  where $c_i$ is the sampled color and $w_i$ is the weight [S1]. The weight is given by:
  $$
  w_i = \Phi\left(\frac{D_i}{t_r}\right) \cdot \Phi\left(-\frac{D_i}{t_r}\right)
  $$
  where $D_i$ is the SDF value, $t_r$ is the truncation distance, and $\Phi$ is the sigmoid function [S1]. The truncation distance cuts off any SDF value too far from individual surfaces [S1].
- **Parameter**: Per-frame appearance latent code from NeRF-W [88] is used to account for white-balance and exposure changes [S1].
- **Pitfall**: Multiple ray-surface intersections are handled by assigning a weight of zero to subsequent truncation regions so they do not contribute to the pixel color [S1].

## Background
The concept of replacing density with SDF in neural radiance fields emerged concurrently in 2021-2022. Azinovic et al. [189] (April 2021) introduced a truncated SDF MLP approach, computing pixel color via weighted sums of sampled colors and using Marching Cubes for mesh extraction [S1]. Concurrently, Park et al. introduced NeuS (November 2020/2021) which established the standard differentiable rendering pipeline for SDFs by converting SDF to density via a cumulative distribution function [S1]. SparseNeuS (June 2022) [207] improved upon NeuS by focusing on sparse-view SDF reconstruction using a geometry encoding volume with learnable image features as a hybrid representation [S1]. These methods collectively shifted the focus from soft volumetric rendering to explicit surface reconstruction within the NeRF framework.
